strengths: Novel conceptual framing: Formulating flow matching post-training as adversarial imitation learning provides an interesting alternative perspective to RLHF/DPO with clear motivation
Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple benchmarks (UniGen, DPG, HPSv3), thorough ablations on discriminator architectures, and extensions to discrete/video generation demonstrate rigor
Strong practical results within scope: Achieves competitive performance with only 13K samples and single expert per prompt (e.g., 87.32 on DPG, outperforming FLUX.1 Ultra)
Well-engineered algorithms: Two complementary approaches (FAIL-PD for white-box differentiable settings, FAIL-PG for black-box scenarios) show solid technical design with stabilization strategies
Clear empirical analysis: Figure 2 and related analysis effectively demonstrate the stability-convergence trade-off, with honest discussion of FAIL-PG collapse behavior
Sound technical execution: Derivations appear correct, connections to DPG and GAIL are well-articulated, and mathematical frameworks are properly developed
weaknesses: Single-step denoising approximation (Eq. 2) lacks rigorous justification: Assumes local linearity of vector field without formal analysis; no ablation comparing to full trajectory backpropagation; sensitivity to Δt unexplored

Severely limited scope with unknown scaling: Only 13K samples with single expert per prompt; paper explicitly acknowledges scaling is 'an open question'; impossible to assess generalization to realistic scenarios
FAIL-PG collapse at 450+ steps is inadequately addressed: Mode-seeking explanation provided but no fundamental solution; undermines practical applicability of the faster algorithm

Significant text rendering gap undermines generalization claims: 52.87 vs 76.14 (Qwen) represents substantial limitation in important downstream tasks; while acknowledged as pretraining-bounded, this severely restricts applicability
Heavy discriminator dependence without principled selection: FAIL-PD shows large sensitivity (DINOv3: 60.65 vs FLUX.1: 62.70); no guidance for practitioners on architecture choice

Questionable baseline implementations: RLHF reward model trained only 1 epoch (likely underfitted); Online DPO with 'perfect discriminator' is somewhat strawman-like; no comparison to recent DPO variants

Lack of human evaluation: Relies entirely on pretrained reward models (circular dependency concern); CFG disabled during evaluation doesn't match typical inference; no statistical significance testing
Insufficient theoretical analysis: No convergence guarantees, sample complexity bounds, or principled guidance on when AIL outperforms preference optimization methods
Extreme hyperparameter sensitivity: Table 10 shows learning rates varying by 10x across settings, suggesting significant tuning was required; reproducibility concerns despite code availability claims
Missing critical ablations: No comparison of single-step vs full trajectory approximation; no analysis of Δt sensitivity; insufficient justification for design choices in FAIL-PD

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation connecting generative model post-training to imitation learning, with clear insight that SFT suffers from behavioral cloning limitations
Thoughtful two-algorithm design with meaningful trade-offs: FAIL-PD for structured gradients and FAIL-PG for flexibility, supported by insightful analysis of mode-seeking vs manifold preservation

Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning multiple benchmarks (UniGen, DPG, HPSv3, UnifiedReward), thorough baseline comparisons (RLHF, DPO), discriminator ablations, and generalization to discrete image and video domains

Practical value demonstrated: achieves improvements with limited data (13K single-sample-per-prompt), shows regularization benefits against reward hacking, and provides both high-performance and computationally flexible options
Clear presentation with effective algorithms, good visualizations, and honest limitations discussion including acknowledgment of data scale constraints and pretraining-induced performance ceiling
weaknesses: Key approximations lack theoretical justification: single-step denoising (Eq. 2) assumes local linearity without error analysis; likelihood ratio approximation (Eq. 3) relies on ELBO tightness without empirical validation; claims of low-variance/unbiased estimates not rigorously proven; no convergence guarantees provided

Experimental scale and design limitations: only 13K examples with single expert per prompt (acknowledged limitation not addressed), no human evaluation despite aesthetic/prompt-following claims, modest performance gaps on some metrics, missing comparisons to other adversarial diffusion methods (DiffusionGAN, UFOGen)

Stability concerns inadequately addressed: Figure 2 shows FAIL-PG mode collapse after 450 steps despite stability claims; method requires multiple stabilization tricks (warmup, hybrid imitation, KL constraints) without individual contribution ablations; hyperparameter sensitivity evident in task-specific learning rates (Table 10)

Critical missing ablations: impact of full-trajectory backpropagation vs. single-step approximation, individual contribution of stabilization strategies, sensitivity to KL coefficient β and step size Δt, comparison to optimal baseline tuning

Under-motivated discriminator selection with performance sensitivity: FLUX-as-discriminator (Table 2: 60.65-62.70 variance) could create problematic gradient dynamics; no principled guidance for practitioners; limited novelty as core technique is DPG+GAIL applied to flow matching

strengths: Novel conceptual framework connecting post-training to adversarial imitation learning with clear motivation and elegant minimax formulation
Thoughtful algorithm design with FAIL-PD exploiting differentiable ODE solvers and FAIL-PG providing black-box alternative; insightful trade-off analysis between convergence speed and stability

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks with thorough ablations on discriminators, data scaling, and initialization; extended training dynamics demonstrating long-term stability
Strong empirical results achieving 73.70 on UniGen-Bench with only 13K demonstrations; demonstrates effectiveness as regularizer against reward hacking when combined with reward models
Successful generalization to discrete image and video generation modalities; extensive implementation details and hyperparameters support reproducibility
weaknesses: Insufficient theoretical justification: one-step denoising approximation (Eq. 2) assumes local linearity without rigorous analysis of optimization landscape impact or convergence guarantees; claimed connection to DPG lacks formal support

Experimental design limitations: single expert sample per prompt and 13K dataset scale raises scalability questions; custom RLHF/DPO baselines may not represent best implementations; missing comparisons with recent methods like Diffusion-DPO

Critical dependence on SFT initialization: Table 15 shows FAIL-PD degrades to 55.23 without SFT cold-start (vs 51.84 baseline), undermining core claim of addressing distribution shift without preference data
High discriminator architecture sensitivity (Table 2: 60.65-62.70 range on UniGen) with no principled guidance for discriminator selection in new domains; unclear what properties are important

Incomplete analysis of adversarial training stability: mode collapse mentioned but not empirically validated; KL masking appears to be a patch; hybrid batch strategy and cold-start are necessary stabilizations
Computational efficiency claims unsupported: FAIL-PG is 1.74× more expensive per step than FAIL-PD with no wall-clock comparison to baselines; memory and scalability to larger models not analyzed
Statistical rigor lacking: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; single runs only; some performance differences small (e.g., 2 points) with unclear significance

Persistent failure modes inadequately analyzed: large gaps in text rendering (52.87 vs 76.14 vs Qwen-Image in Table 7) acknowledged but not systematically investigated; unclear when method succeeds vs. fails
